The Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Prof. Joash Amupitan, has defended the use of artificial intelligence in election management, saying the technology is not a threat to democracy despite its potential misuse by malicious actors. Amupitan said AI could improve electoral administration through efficient voter registration, logistics planning, data analysis and the management of large voter databases, while warning that advances in generative AI had made it easier to create deceptive content capable of undermining public confidence in elections. The INEC chairman spoke on Monday at The Beyond the Ballot Summit in Abuja, where he explained that electoral management bodies worldwide had adopted AI-assisted processes to improve administrative efficiency and strengthen election planning. He said, “Artificial Intelligence, AI, is not an enemy of democracy.” He, however, expressed concern over the growing accessibility of generative AI tools, which he said could be exploited to manipulate voters and spread disinformation during elections. These tools target specific vulnerabilities with distinct timelines,” he said. The INEC chairman’s remarks come amid preparations for the 2027 general election, with the commission recently announcing plans to integrate AI into Nigeria’s electoral system. The growing use of AI in electoral processes has heightened concerns about the spread of fabricated announcements, manipulated audio recordings and realistic videos that could mislead voters, impersonate public officials and disrupt election administration. While the technology offers opportunities to improve the efficiency of election management, its potential misuse presents challenges for electoral integrity, particularly in an environment where false information can spread rapidly through social media. INEC’s planned adoption of AI therefore places renewed emphasis on the need to balance technological innovation with safeguards against misinformation, impersonation and other forms of digital manipulation. The commission noted that it would ensure that the technology strengthens the credibility, transparency and efficiency of the electoral process as Nigeria approaches the 2027 polls. The controversy over the use of AI in elections intensified recently after suspicious photographs, including images believed to have been AI-generated, were found in INEC’s preliminary Register of Voters. The photographs, which appeared in some voter records in Etsako West Local Government Area of Edo State, raised questions about the integrity of the voter database and the processes used to capture and verify registration information. INEC subsequently acknowledged the questionable records and said it was investigating the circumstances surrounding the photographs. The commission’s Director of Information and Communication Technology, Lawrence Bayode, said some of the AI-generated images were linked to irregularities allegedly introduced by some registration officers who had access to the system. INEC has stressed that the register remains preliminary and subject to verification, data cleaning and correction before the final register is certified.
